catalog_locator: 'The Accent', p.7; immediate future tense, p.49
catalog_quote: THE ACCENT. The accent is invariably on the last syllable but one. When two vowels come together they are usually pronounced as close vowels, in which case the accent is thrown back to the first of these vowels, as ku-leiUiy [scanned-garbled example] to dun. When a suffix is used the accent is moved so as to be on the last syllable but one. There are but few monosyllabic words in the Sagalla dialect. ... [p.49] The immediate future is formed by the use of the same pronominal prefixes as in the mediate future, but without the syllable ./e- [scanned for je-], and slightly throwing the accent on the final syllable of the verb, as — ni-lima, I will cultivate. The final -a of this tense is often changed into -a^ga [scanned for -a'ga], as — ni-lim-a'gay [scanned for ni-lim-a'ga,] I will cultivate.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the held Wray 1894 djvu text at printed p.7 and p.49; the p.7 page image fetched sources now confirms the wording and fixes the garbled example ('ku-leila, to dun'). (2) The classification rests on an 1894 SPCK missionary primer (pedagogical grammar/sketch) with an impressionistic, tone-blind 'accent' statement. For Sagalla proper Glottolog lists nothing better (2 refs: Wray 1894; unpublished Verbi & Austin notes), and repository searches (UoN, KU) found no Sagalla phonology thesis (the held UoN 2016 MA is a loanword study; its bibliography cites Mwasusu 2012 on Kidawida stress, a different language). However Breteler 2018's bibliography and Crossref show modern tone-focused fieldwork on Saghala by Patin (2002 MA thesis on the 'systeme accentuel'; 2009 Faits de Langues article), neither held nor open; held Breteler 2018 relays Patin's data
